transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jin Park (Nova CTO), Priya Rao (Nova SRE), Liam Chen (Nova ML)

Summary: quick deep-dive on p95/p99 tail latency, streaming vs non-streaming, KV cache warm/cold behaviour, batching tradeoffs, quantization impact on latency and CPU/GPU memcpy, and network hops when using VPC/private deployment. Agreed to run bench and share logs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we want to focus today on tail latency—p95 and p99—specifically the things that surprise folks when they first move to production, like KV cache warm-ups, batching, and network hops. Quick intros?
[00:10] Jin (Nova CTO): Hi, Jin here. We're seeing spikes in p99 that are causing timeouts in our orchestration. We run a mix of short queries ~30 tokens and long--like 1k tokens on occasion.
[00:22] Priya (Nova SRE): Yeah, we've seen occasional 800ms spikes when most responses are 120-200ms. Not sure if it's GPU queuing or network.
[00:30] Samir (Redwood SE): Got it. One framing: p95 often driven by batching and kernel scheduling, p99 more by cold KV cache, context switching, and network path variability. We'll try to map each.
[00:45] Liam (Nova ML): One question up front - we use a VPC private deployment option and route requests through a proxy–so extra hops there, TLS terminate at the proxy. Could that be the cause?
[00:55] Alex: Absolutely could. TLS handshake and connection setup matter a lot. Keep-alive and connection pooling remove that hit for steady traffic.
[01:10] Priya: We do short lived connections from Kubernetes pods, we might not be reusing TCP connections properly.
[01:20] Samir: That'd show up as higher cold-start percentiles. For the KV cache: cold cache means we fetch KV from storage - that can add 100s ms depending on where it's stored. Redwoods runtime tries to keep KV local on GPU memory - but on a miss it's a path to disk or remote node.
[01:40] Jin: Can you explain the KV cache warm/cold behaviour again? What's 'local' vs 'remote' misses?
[01:47] Samir: Sure. Local means the KV sits in the GPU-local cache (same process / GPU memory). Remote miss means the system needs to fetch KV from another host or read from persistent store. With NVLink/PCIe transfers between GPUs, cross-host reads add a lot. Also fragmentation in cache eviction can cause misses.
[02:05] Alex: And you might see that as a p99 spike only for certain prefixes if user sessions are spread.
[02:12] Liam: We also use batching windows tuned to 20ms; sometimes batching increases latency for short queries, but reduces cost. Should we change it?
[02:22] Samir: It's a classic tradeoff. Dynamic batching helps; for low-latency short queries set smaller max batch size and low wait window. But bursty traffic can cause queueing. For p99 it's important to watch queue length histograms.
[02:38] Priya: Any quantization tips? We're currently using int8 quantized models in staging. We saw marginal latency improvement but sometimes increased variance.
[02:48] Samir: Int8 gives throughput improvements but sometimes kernel selection falls back to slower code paths for certain layer shapes. You may hit a mismatch in kernel codegen that causes rare slow paths. Int4/act-order quantization can reduce memory bandwidth and help, but depends on backend.
[03:05] Alex: Also, quantization reduces compute time but increases sensitivity to memory copy overhead. So if your workflow has CPU->GPU memcpy per request, the relative impact on tail can be higher.
[03:20] Jin: We've got a pretty standard egress path: app pods -> sidecar proxy -> NAT gateway -> Redwood VPC endpoint. Multi-hop and NATing seems suspect. Any idea how to measure the contribution?
[03:34] Samir: We usually instrument RTTs at three points: app->proxy, proxy->gateway, gateway->redwood endpoint. If you have distributed tracing you can attach timestamps on request entry and exit. For TCP-level you can capture SYN/ACK RTTs, but TLS handshake time and cert validation add cost.
[03:50] Alex: For streaming vs non-streaming: streaming can lower first-byte latency because server can flush tokens as they're generated, but it exposes tail variance from network chunking and gRPC flow control. Non-streaming gets whole response serialized and sent, which can hide internal token generation variability but increases time to first token.
[04:13] Priya: So for our chat UI where first token shows typing, streaming is better. But our p99s spike when multiple large requests are in flight.
[04:24] Samir: Right—concurrency with streaming increases pressure on KV caches and slots. Also, if you do server-side streaming over HTTP/1.1 chunked vs HTTP/2 or gRPC, you can get different behavior for head-of-line blocking.
[04:40] Liam: Any kernel-level hints? We saw some odd slow CUDA memcpy calls occasionally.
[04:46] Samir: Those memcpy spikes are often PCIe saturation or PCIe bus contention when multiple GPUs share host. Also, CPU scheduling can cause jitter when memory copies are initiated by different threads. Using pinned memory and prefetching helps. We can share a checklist.
[05:00] Alex: We should mention quantize path selection: our compiler chooses kernels based on sequence length distribution. If your workload is mostly short sequences but occasionally very long sequences, we can get a path switch which may evict compiled kernels and cause extra compile time or synchronization. That shows up in p99.
[05:20] Jin: That's interesting. We do have a small amount of very long context runs (2-4k) for retrieval-augmented generation. Could that cause compile/regeneration overhead?
[05:30] Samir: Yes. Pre-warming those code paths or pinning a model variant for long-context runs helps. We can also precompile kernels for expected lengths.
[05:40] Priya: On the networking front, what's the impact of VPC peering vs PrivateLink type endpoint?
[05:47] Alex: VPC peering can add routing hops and depends on route tables. PrivateLink (or interface endpoints) keeps traffic inside AWS' internal network with less NATing, generally lower latency and more predictable. If you have heavy cross-region traffic, that's the bigger factor.
[06:03] Jin: We're single region right now (us-west-2) but we have a cross-AZ setup.
[06:09] Samir: Cross-AZ adds microseconds but can add variance under load because traffic may get retransmitted across fabric. For p99 it's small but not negligible. More important is whether requests sometimes get routed to a cold host or LAZY-provisioned node.
[06:24] Liam: How about connection reuse in the SDK? We use short-lived Lambda functions for some tasks. Does Lambda cold start plus connection setup show up?
[06:33] Samir: Definitely. Lambdas that create a new TLS connection per invocation will add 100-200ms per cold connection. Use connection pooling or a warm container strategy. For many customers that was the single largest p99 source.
[06:46] Priya: Regarding caching: what's the expected hit rate delta to meaningfully reduce p99?
[06:52] Samir: If you can get your KV hit rate above ~85-90% for prefix-heavy workloads you'll see big improvements because remote fetches go from 100-300ms extra down to near-zero. But it depends on session stickiness.
[07:10] Alex: We saw a customer reduce p99 from 1.2s to 320ms by improving KV locality and switching to persistent connections.
[07:20] Jin: Nice. Any tools we can run on our side to profile kernel hotspots?
[07:25] Samir: We'll share a perf harness (link to internal sheet) — it collects per-token timings, NVTX markers, and kernel durations. You can run on a sample fleet or on dedicated test hosts. We'll also send a lightweight profiler you can run in-prod with low overhead.
[07:40] Priya: About batching, are there recommended batch size caps for 1-2 token prompts vs long generation?
[07:46] Samir: For very short prompts keep max batch size small (4-8) and wait window 5-10ms. For long generations you can increase batch size because generation amortises cost. Also, adaptive batching that distinguishes request type is best.
[08:02] Liam: Does Redwood support adaptive batching per route?
[08:05] Alex: Yes—per-route batching config. You can define routes for chat vs completion and set different windows and max batch sizes.
[08:12] Jin: If we go Dedicated, will we be able to control kernel selection or quantization profile?
[08:17] Samir: Dedicated gives you a lot of knobs: quantization presets, kernel flags, and ability to pin model versions. We can also expose a compile cache so you can stage precompiled kernels for your workloads.
[08:30] Priya: Security question — if we use private deployment on-prem, how does KMS/HSM integration affect latency?
[08:36] Alex: KMS calls happen mainly at key unwrap time (session startup). After that keys are cached in memory or HSM session kept alive. If you do per-request KMS, that will add significant latency. With proper integration, per-request overhead is negligible.
[08:52] Jin: We have strict audit logging requirements - will adding heavy logging affect latency?
[08:58] Samir: If logging is synchronous it can impact tail latency. We recommend async logging and batch writes for audit events. Also, sampling of heavy telemetry is important.
[09:10] Priya: Back to actual numbers — can you walk through a sample p95/p99 breakdown?
[09:14] Samir: Sure. Example ribbon: median ~120ms, p95 ~220ms, p99 ~560ms. Attribution: network-> 30% of p99, queueing/batching-> 25%, cold KV fetch-> 30%, kernel/regeneration/compile-> 15%. Those are illustrative but show multiple contributors.
[09:36] Liam: For streaming, does chunked transfer increase p99 more than non-stream?
[09:40] Samir: It can, because chunk flushes depend on token generation bursts and network pacing. But streamed p99 for first byte can be lower while last byte variance may be higher. It trades off perceived latency vs end-to-end consistency.
[09:56] Alex: We're going to propose a plan: Redwood will run bench with your sample traffic, instrument per-hop latencies, and deliver a breakdown. We'll also test streaming vs non-streaming, and run cold vs warm cache profiles.
[10:10] Priya: Sounds good. For bench infra, what do you need from us?
[10:15] Samir: Sample prompts, distribution of short/long, expected RPS, and a sample set of sessions for session stickiness. Also network topology: are you NATing, do you have egress proxies, privateLink vs peering.
[10:28] Jin: We'll get that over. Also we'd appreciate a checklist for reducing p99 quickly.
[10:34] Alex: We'll attach a short ops checklist: enable keep-alive, connection pool, set batching per-route, pre-warm long-context model paths, and move KV to local GPU-resident store where possible.
[10:48] Liam: One last quick question - are there known pathological cases with quantization + streaming?
[10:53] Samir: Rarely, some quantized kernels have higher jitter on long sequences due to operand packing and fallback to slower kernels for odd token alignments. We'll test your model variant.
[11:05] Priya: Great. Recap and next steps?
[11:08] Alex: Recap - Redwood runs benchmarks (streaming & non-streaming), share perf logs and checklist, Nova provides sample workloads and network topology, we aim to reconvene in one week. Action items in the calendar invite.
[11:20] Jin: Thanks all.
[11:24] Alex: Thanks, we'll follow up.

Notes: occasional transcript artifacts: 'K V cache' or 'kv cache' present, Samir pronounced some kernel names oddly; some timestamps approximate. References shared: perf-harness sheet (link: https://redwood.internal/perf-harness), ops-checklist deck (link: https://redwood.docs/ops-checklist), SOC2 summary (link: https://redwood.docs/soc2-summary).
